newsitem.title: USA: U.S. welfare roll drop validates changes - Clinton.
newsitem.headline: U.S. welfare roll drop validates changes - Clinton.

text.p: President Clinton said Tuesday a one-year decline of 1.4 million in the number of people on welfare showed changes in the system had worked.
An aide, however, admitted that there was no proof the government overhaul had caused the drop.

Clinton also worked Tuesday for the welfare of the debt-ridden Democratic Party. He was to raise about $550,000 for party coffers by attending events in St. Louis and Washington before the day was done.

Speaking in the sauna-like heat of an old warehouse on a steamy August day, Clinton said the nation's welfare caseload had fallen by 1.4 million recipients in the year since he had signed a Republican-backed welfare law.
The law ended the federal government's guarantee of federal aid and led to dire predictions about the future of the underprivileged.
"I heard all the reasons that people said it wouldn't work. But a year later, I think it's fair to say the debate is over. We know now that welfare reform works," Clinton said.

Since he took office in January 1993, the number of people receiving welfare benefits fell by 24 percent, or 3.4 million recipients. Clinton called the decline in the welfare rolls the largest ever in the United States.

But his chief domestic policy adviser, Bruce Reed, acknowledged there was no statistical proof that the welfare changes had caused the sharp decline. He noted that it would be five years before the full implications of the law could be measured.

Discussing the people who left the benefit rolls in the past year, Reed said: "Most of these people have probably gone to work or gotten married. ... We won't know all the facts on this for some time to come."
In Washington, Brookings Institution analyst Robert Reischauer said the drop had more to do with the robust U.S. economy and the flexibility Clinton gave states to administer their programmes.

"The strength of the economy has obviously been a major factor explaining the drop in the welfare rolls," he said, adding, "It is premature to attribute much of the drop in the rolls to the welfare bill because ... the consequences of those changes in most states probably haven't been implemented yet."
The new welfare law includes requirements that able-bodied welfare recipents find work within two years and that people on welfare receive benefits for no more than five years.

A state-by-state analysis released by the White House on the decline in welfare rolls since 1993 showed wide differences between states. Eleven saw rolls go down 40 percent or more, led by Wyoming with a 68 percent drop, while California's dropped 1 percent and New York's went down 12 percent. Hawaii's welfare caseloads increased by 36 percent, and Alaska's went up 5 percent.

Clinton made his remarks on welfare to work trainees, former welfare recipients and local business leaders at a daylong Welfare-to-Work Partnership meeting in a warehouse bought for future worker training by a consortium of 250 companies.
He also appeared at a fund-raising luncheon with House Democratic leader Dick Gephardt of Missouri, a likely rival to Vice President Al Gore for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2000.

Clinton sought to play down his differences with Gephardt, who opposed both the welfare bill last year and the balanced budget legislation the president signed last week. Instead he urged the audience to give control of the House back to Democrats in elections next year.
"We are within sight of winning the majority in the House," Clinton proclaimed at the affair, which raised $250,000 for the Democratic National Committee.

Both Clinton and Gore spoke Tuesday night in Washington at a Democratic National Committee Leadership Conference dinner that raised another $300,000. Some of the contributions at both events were large, unregulated "soft money" donations of the sort that Clinton has said he wants to ban under campaign finance legislation stalled in Congress.
